claim: Intracellular factors can be inherited across cellular generations, giving rise to correlation patterns in cell cycle timing between cells of different family relationships on lineage trees.
source: These factors can be inherited across cellular generations which gives rise to, often non-intuitive, correlation patterns in cell cycle timing between cells of different family relationships on lineage trees.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a key premise of the work.

claim: The framework reveals three distinct interdivision time correlation patterns: aperiodic, alternator, and oscillator.
source: Here, we formulate a framework of hidden inherited factors affecting the cell cycle that unifies known cell cycle control models and reveals three distinct interdivision time correlation patterns: aperiodic, alternator, and oscillator.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and demonstrated throughout the results.

claim: Interdivision time correlation patterns do not identify a single cell cycle model but generally admit a broad posterior distribution of possible mechanisms.
source: From our inference, we find that interdivision time correlation patterns do not identify a single cell cycle model but generally admit a broad posterior distribution of possible mechanisms.
evidence: This is a key finding from the Bayesian inference analysis presented in the results.

claim: Cell cycle factors are commonly driven by circadian rhythms.
source: This reveals that cell cycle factors are commonly driven by circadian rhythms, but their period may differ in cancer.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of multiple datasets showing oscillatory patterns consistent with circadian periods.

claim: The period of cell cycle factors may differ in cancer.
source: This reveals that cell cycle factors are commonly driven by circadian rhythms, but their period may differ in cancer.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis of human colorectal cancer data showing different oscillator periods.

claim: Stochastic gene expression can lead to heterogeneity in cell cycle length.
source: For example, stochastic gene expression (Elowitz et al., 2002) can lead to heterogeneity in cell cycle length (Kiviet et al., 2014; Ghusinga et al., 2016; Thomas et al., 2018) as these fluctuations can be propagated by concerted cellular cues (Co et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The cousin-mother inequality describes a correlation pattern where interdivision times of cousin cells are more correlated than those of mother-daughter pairs.
source: A counter-intuitive correlation pattern presented by many cell types is the 'cousin-mother inequality' (Sandler et al., 2015), where the interdivision times of cousin cells are more correlated than those of mother-daughter pairs.
evidence: This is a definition of a known phenomenon with citation support.

claim: The cousin-mother inequality can be observed both in bacteria and mammalian cells.
source: This inequality can be observed both in bacteria and mammalian cells (Figure 1b).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: Simple inheritance rules with a single parameter cannot explain the lineage correlation patterns seen in experimental single-cell data.
source: Previous studies (Cowan and Staudte, 1986; Sandler et al., 2015) found that simple inheritance rules, where interdivision times are correlated from one generation to another through a single parameter, cannot explain the lineage correlation patterns seen in experimental single-cell data.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The interdivision time is determined by a number of cell cycle factors that represent hidden variables.
source: To address this issue, we propose a unified framework where the interdivision time is determined by a number of cell cycle factors that represent hidden variables such as cell cycle phase lengths, protein levels, cell growth rate or other unknowns (Figure 1c), that each have their own inheritance pattern.
evidence: This is the core model proposed in the paper.

claim: The inheritance matrix model includes many known cell cycle models as a special case.
source: The general model (Equation 1a and b) includes many known cell cycle models as a special case.
evidence: This is stated as a property of the proposed model with examples given in the appendix.

claim: The aperiodic pattern is characterized by real positive eigenvalues of the inheritance matrix.
source: These can be classified by the eigenvalues of the inheritance matrix θ: (i) if the inheritance matrix exhibits real positive eigenvalues, we observe an aperiodic pattern (Figure 2d)
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived from the model and demonstrated in Figure 2d.

claim: The alternator pattern is characterized by real eigenvalues with at least one negative eigenvalue.
source: (ii) if the inheritance matrix has real eigenvalues with at least one negative eigenvalue, we observe an alternator pattern (Figure 2e)
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived from the model and demonstrated in Figure 2e.

claim: The oscillator pattern is characterized by a pair of complex eigenvalues.
source: (iii) if there is a pair of complex eigenvalues we observe an oscillator pattern (Figure 2f)
evidence: This is a theoretical result derived from the model and demonstrated in Figure 2f.

claim: All three correlation patterns can be compatible with the cousin-mother inequality if N≥2.
source: We find that this is not the case, but instead, all three correlation patterns can be compatible with the cousin-mother inequality if N≥2.
evidence: This is demonstrated through theoretical analysis shown in Figure 2m-o.

claim: Oscillations can arise even in parameter regions that violate the cousin-mother inequality.
source: Interestingly, we find that oscillations can arise even in parameter regions that violate the cousin-mother inequality (Figure 2o).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2o.

claim: The one-dimensional model (N=1) provides a poor fit for datasets that display the cousin-mother inequality.
source: We found that the model fit is poor for the datasets that display the cousin-mother inequality, which is the case for cyanobacteria, clock-deleted cyanobacteria, neuroblastoma and human colorectal cancer cells (Appendix 1—figure 1a–f).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Bayesian inference results shown in Appendix 1—figure 1.

claim: Mycobacteria is the only cell type that has a good fit for the one-dimensional model.
source: The only cell type that has a good fit for the one-dimensional model is mycobacteria (Appendix 1—figure 1c).
evidence: This is shown through model fitting results in Appendix 1—figure 1c.

claim: The two-dimensional inheritance matrix model provides a good fit for all six datasets.
source: Bayesian inference (Materials and methods - 'Data analysis and Bayesian inference of the inheritance matrix model') produced a good model fit for all six datasets (Figure 3a–f) for the two-factor inheritance matrix model, within relatively narrow error bars of mother, grandmother, sister and cousin correlations (Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through the fitting results shown in Figure 3.

claim: The AIC values indicate that the inheritance matrix model with two cell cycle factors provides the simplest fit for all cell types except mycobacteria.
source: The AIC values indicate that the inheritance matrix model with two cell cycle factors provides the simplest fit for all cell types used here, except for the mycobacteria data where simple inheritance rules provided an equally good fit with a significant reduction in the number of model parameters.
evidence: This is based on AIC calculations shown in Appendix 1—table 1.

claim: The model has good predictive capacity for correlations further down the lineage tree.
source: Crucially, we find that the model has a good predictive capacity for correlations further down the lineage tree.
evidence: This is demonstrated by the model's ability to predict great-grandmother and great-great-grandmother correlations not used in fitting.

claim: Cyanobacteria display a dominant oscillator pattern with 100% posterior probability.
source: Cyanobacteria, (Figure 3a), human colorectal cancer (Figure 3d), and mouse embryonic fibroblasts (Figure 3f) display a dominant oscillator pattern
evidence: This is shown in the bar chart in Figure 3a.

claim: Clock-deleted cyanobacteria display a 100% alternator pattern.
source: We see that clock-deleted cyanobacteria (Figure 3b) has a 100% alternator pattern in contrast to the 100% oscillator pattern seen for wild type cyanobacteria
evidence: This is shown in the bar chart in Figure 3b.

claim: Deletion of the clock gene has completely transformed the correlation pattern and abolished the underlying oscillation in cyanobacteria.
source: suggesting that the deletion of the clock gene has completely transformed the correlation pattern and has abolished the underlying oscillation.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing wild type and clock-deleted cyanobacteria patterns.

claim: Neuroblastoma displays a dominant aperiodic pattern.
source: Neuroblastoma (Figure 3e) displays a dominant aperiodic pattern.
evidence: This is shown in the bar chart in Figure 3e.

claim: Individual inheritance parameters are not identifiable from interdivision time correlation patterns.
source: We found that the explorations of the Gibbs sampler did not settle in a particular parameter subspace but meandered off to explore vast areas of the parameter space without improving the likelihood values (Appendix 1—figure 3a and b). Such behaviour is expected when model parameters are not identifiable
evidence: This is demonstrated through MCMC sampling behavior shown in Appendix 1—figure 3 and Figure 4.

claim: The eigenvalues of the inheritance matrix are identifiable while individual parameters are not.
source: In contrast to the individual parameters, the sampled posterior distribution of the eigenvalues is consistent across the averages (Figure 4c) and their mean squared displacement converges rapidly (Figure 4d).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 4c and 4d comparing parameter vs eigenvalue sampling behavior.

claim: Interdivision time correlations alone are insufficient to gain mechanistic insights into cell cycle control mechanisms.
source: This finding suggests that interdivision time correlations alone are insufficient to gain mechanistic insights into cell cycle control mechanisms.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the unidentifiability of individual parameters.

claim: Clock-deleted cyanobacteria and neuroblastoma have distinct hidden correlation patterns of cell cycle factors.
source: Thus, the different interdivision time correlation patterns observed for clock-deleted cyanobacteria and neuroblastoma stem from distinct hidden correlation patterns of cell cycle factor fluctuations.
evidence: This is inferred from the analysis shown in Figure 4f-h.

claim: The period of the correlation oscillation does not always match the frequency of the underlying oscillator.
source: The resolution to this issue is that the period of the correlation oscillation does not always match the frequency of the underlying oscillator.
evidence: This is a theoretical finding explained through Equation 7 and Figure 5a.

claim: There exists a number of oscillators that can all explain the same correlation pattern.
source: Our finding has fundamental implications for the reconstruction of oscillator periods from interdivision time data, revealing that there exists a number of oscillators that can all explain the same correlation pattern.
evidence: This is derived from the theoretical analysis of Equation 7.

claim: The median period of correlation oscillations is 41.7 hr for cyanobacteria.
source: Using these distributions, we estimate the median period of the correlation oscillations (using Equation 6) to be 41.7 hr for cyanobacteria
evidence: This is calculated from the posterior distribution shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The median period of correlation oscillations is 144.3 hr for fibroblasts.
source: we estimate the median period of the correlation oscillations (using Equation 6) to be 41.7 hr for cyanobacteria and 144.3 hr for fibroblasts (Figure 5d).
evidence: This is calculated from the posterior distribution shown in Figure 5d.

claim: The finding of circadian periods supports a strong coupling of circadian rhythms to the cell cycle in cyanobacteria and fibroblasts.
source: This finding supports a strong coupling of circadian rhythms to the cell cycle, as reported previously for both cyanobacteria (Yang et al., 2010; Martins et al., 2018) and fibroblasts (Nagoshi et al., 2004; Menger et al., 2007; Nagoshi et al., 2005).
evidence: This conclusion is supported by the inferred oscillator periods and previous literature.

claim: The dominant correlation pattern in human colorectal cancer was oscillatory with 78% posterior probability.
source: The dominant correlation pattern was oscillatory (78% posterior probability, Figure 3d, bar chart).
evidence: This is shown in the bar chart in Figure 3d.

claim: The posterior distribution of complex eigenvalues for human colorectal cancer has two distribution modes depending on whether the eigenvalues have positive or negative real parts.
source: The posterior distribution of complex eigenvalues for the oscillator pattern has support in a large region of the parameter space. It has two distribution modes depending on whether the eigenvalues have positive or negative real parts (Figure 5f).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5f.

claim: Cluster A in human colorectal cancer has a median correlation oscillation period of 51.2 hr.
source: Cluster A has a median correlation oscillation period of 51.2 hr
evidence: This is calculated from the posterior distribution shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Cluster B in human colorectal cancer has a median correlation oscillation period of 100.6 hr.
source: while cluster B has a median period of 100.6 hr (Figure 5g).
evidence: This is calculated from the posterior distribution shown in Figure 5g.

claim: Cluster B in human colorectal cancer has a median oscillator period T₋₁ of 19.6 hr.
source: The majority of posterior samples, cluster B, had a different predicted period with a median of 19.6 hr (Figure 5h).
evidence: This is calculated from the posterior distribution shown in Figure 5h.

claim: About 33% of posterior samples with complex eigenvalues in human colorectal cancer were assigned to cluster A.
source: However, only about 33% of posterior samples with complex eigenvalues were assigned to this cluster.
evidence: This is stated based on the clustering analysis shown in Figure 5g.

claim: The circadian period may be shortened in cancer cells.
source: A possible explanation is that the circadian period is shortened in cancer cells.
evidence: This is speculated based on the 19.6 hr oscillator period found in cluster B.

claim: Several studies report periods of 18 hr and 20 hr for gene expressions in the human colorectal cancer core-clock.
source: Indeed, several studies report similar periods of 18 hr and 20 hr for gene expressions in the human colorectal cancer core-clock (Fuhr et al., 2019; Parascandolo et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The oscillator correlation pattern predicts a negative grandmother correlation while the alternator pattern predicts a positive grandmother correlation in human colorectal cancer.
source: We found that the oscillator correlation pattern predicts a negative grandmother correlation while the alternator pattern predicts a positive grandmother correlation (Figure 5i and j).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5i and j.

claim: Posterior samples in cluster A predicted a positive interdivision time correlation between a cell and its great-grandmother, while cluster B predicted a negative correlation.
source: Posterior samples in cluster A predicted a positive interdivision time correlation between a cell and its great-grandmother, while cluster B predicted a negative correlation (Figure 5k and l).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5k and l.

claim: Lineage tree correlation patterns of cyanobacteria, mouse embryonic fibroblasts and human colorectal cancer can be explained through an underlying circadian oscillator coupled to cell division.
source: An important result of the present analysis is that lineage tree correlation patterns of very different cell types – cyanobacteria, mouse embryonic fibroblasts and human colorectal cancer – can be explained through an underlying circadian oscillator coupled to cell division.
evidence: This is a key conclusion drawn from the analysis of oscillator periods in these datasets.

claim: The method robustly reconstructs the circadian rhythms from the interdivision time correlation patterns despite the lack of the cousin-mother inequality for fibroblasts.
source: Our method robustly reconstructs the circadian rhythms from the interdivision time correlation patterns despite the lack of the cousin-mother inequality for fibroblasts
evidence: This demonstrates the method's capability shown in the fibroblast analysis.

claim: Cyanobacteria are characterized by complex eigenvalues with negative real parts.
source: They are characterised by complex eigenvalues with negative real parts in cyanobacteria, but positive real parts in fibroblasts (Figure 5c)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c.

claim: Fibroblasts are characterized by complex eigenvalues with positive real parts.
source: They are characterised by complex eigenvalues with negative real parts in cyanobacteria, but positive real parts in fibroblasts (Figure 5c)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5c.

claim: The circadian clock in fibroblasts relies on transcriptional mechanisms.
source: While the circadian clock in fibroblasts relies on transcriptional mechanisms (Hughes et al., 2009; Menger et al., 2007; Takahashi, 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The origin of the clock is non-transcriptional in cyanobacteria.
source: the origin of the clock is non-transcriptional in cyanobacteria (Cohen and Golden, 2015; Tomita et al., 2005; Nakajima et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The negative mother-daughter correlation in cyanobacteria likely stems from size control mechanisms that are modulated by the circadian clock.
source: The negative mother-daughter correlation in cyanobacteria likely stems from size control mechanisms that are modulated by the circadian clock (Martins et al., 2018).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation.

claim: The result extends the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem to lineage trees.
source: Our result thus extends the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem to lineage trees.
evidence: This is a theoretical contribution connecting the findings to signal processing theory.

claim: HES1 expression oscillates with a period of around 5 h in human colon cancer cells.
source: For example, HES1 expression oscillates with a period of around 5 h in human colon cancer cells (William et al., 2007; Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NF-κB oscillates with a period of approximately 100 min.
source: The stress response regulators NF-κB and p53, which are critical for tumour development, oscillate with periods of approximately 100 min and 5 hr, respectively (Harper et al., 2018; Stewart-Ornstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: p53 oscillates with a period of approximately 5 hr.
source: The stress response regulators NF-κB and p53, which are critical for tumour development, oscillate with periods of approximately 100 min and 5 hr, respectively (Harper et al., 2018; Stewart-Ornstein et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Correlation patterns are an emergent phenomenon that impact cell proliferation.
source: Our quantitative analysis thus reveals that correlation patterns are an emergent phenomenon that impact cell proliferation and these patterns may be altered in disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall analysis.

claim: Correlation patterns may be altered in disease.
source: Our quantitative analysis thus reveals that correlation patterns are an emergent phenomenon that impact cell proliferation and these patterns may be altered in disease.
evidence: This is suggested by the differences observed in cancer cell data.
